analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on multinational corporations that bring overseas profits back to the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee; with zero cosponsors, it received no action and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let US multinational corporations pay roughly a quarter of the normal tax rate on foreign profits they bring home, instead of the full rate. To earn the break, a company would have to keep its US workforce from shrinking over the next two years — losing employees would add income back to its taxes at $75,000 per missing worker — and companies that grow their payrolls beyond 2014 levels would get an extra deduction. The bill was introduced by Representative Trent Franks with no cosponsors and died in the Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: US multinational corporations with large piles of untaxed foreign earnings would gain the most: they could bring those profits home while paying roughly 25% of the normal corporate tax rate on them. Shareholders would benefit through the cash windfall, and workers would benefit only to the extent that companies actually grew payrolls above 2014 levels, which would earn a modest extra deduction — and companies would owe $75,000 per lost full-time US worker if they shrank employment after taking the break.

how_it_helps.text: It amends section 965 of the tax code to let US parent companies deduct 75% of dividends received from their foreign subsidiaries, so those repatriated earnings would be taxed at roughly a quarter of the normal rate.

Companies get an additional bonus deduction — up to 10% of the repatriated dividends — in the year after the election, but only if their total payroll grows above its 2014 level; a company that merely keeps employment steady gets no bonus but also no penalty.

A clawback provision adds income of $75,000 per employee below the company's prior average US employment level if it sheds full-time American workers in the 24 months after taking the tax break, capped at the total deduction claimed.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect far less tax on billions of dollars of repatriated foreign profits, with the shortfall borne by other taxpayers or by higher deficits. Because the employment condition only penalizes companies that shrink their US workforce below prior levels — not companies that fail to hire — the public gets no guarantee of new jobs in exchange for the tax cut.

drawbacks.text: The bill would give a deep tax cut (a 75% deduction on repatriated dividends) to multinational corporations with the largest stock of untaxed offshore profits, reducing federal revenue.

The employment conditions are weak: a company avoids any penalty by simply keeping its existing US workforce steady, and the bonus deduction is capped at 10% of the repatriated amount — so the main benefit flows whether or not new jobs are created.

The bill would allow companies to elect the deduction for their last taxable year beginning before enactment or their first year beginning within a year after, a broad window that invites large one-time tax benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a corporate tax cut with a jobs string attached, and the string is weak. Employing anyone in the United States — even without adding a single job — avoids the clawback, and only full payroll growth earns the modest bonus deduction. Meanwhile the entire base of offshore earnings is taxed at a fraction of the normal rate, a permanent transfer of tax revenue to the companies that have the most profit parked abroad. The 2004 version of this kind of holiday (section 965, the same statute this bill amends) is widely understood to have produced mostly share buybacks and dividends rather than new hiring, and this bill carries the same design risk.

outcome.mechanism: A single representative introduced it and no one signed on; the tax-writing committee never took it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2015 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No representative signed on as a cosponsor.
The full action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers are better off, because the tax cut never happened; no domestic interest lost anything of value.

for.name: Rep. Trent Franks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 5, 2015; it was referred to Ways and Means the same day.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on, so there is no record of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations with large offshore profits
industries.note: The bill would let these companies repatriate foreign earnings at roughly a quarter of the normal tax rate, with only a modest bonus tied to payroll growth and a clawback if they cut US jobs. The 2004 repatriation holiday under the same tax-code section is widely understood to have sent most of the money to share buybacks and dividends rather than hiring.
A 75% deduction on repatriated foreign dividends would reduce tax revenue, leaving other taxpayers to make up the difference unless the money produced taxable economic gains.
